lines.text: Total student debt: about $1.50 trillion in 2019 to about $1.66 trillion in 2026 (Q3).
lines.say: And the pile keeps growing. Total student debt went from about one point five trillion dollars in twenty nineteen to about one point six six trillion in twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: The Q3 2026 reading: $1.656 trillion.
lines.say: The latest reading, from the third quarter of twenty twenty-six, was one point six five six trillion dollars.

lines.text: Meanwhile, a 2025 law rewrote federal repayment, and much of it kicked in July 1, 2026.
lines.say: Meanwhile, a twenty twenty-five law rewrote federal repayment, and much of it kicked in on July first, twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: The law was signed in July 2025. A new plan, RAP, opened in July 2026.
lines.say: The law was signed in July twenty twenty-five, and a new plan called RAP opened in July twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: More changes roll in through 2028, so some advice online is already out of date.
lines.say: More changes roll in through twenty twenty-eight, so some online advice is already out of date.

lines.text: The road map: know your loans, pick a plan, check forgiveness, pay it down faster.
lines.say: So here's the road map: know your loans, pick a plan, check forgiveness, and pay it down faster.

lines.text: Then the traps: refinancing, default, and scammers who charge for free help. Plus a checklist.
lines.say: Then the traps: refinancing, default, and the scammers who charge for free help. Plus a checklist at the end.

lines.text: This is education, not advice, and every number comes with its date.

lines.text: Chapter 1: Know what you owe.
lines.say: Chapter one: know what you owe.

lines.text: Step one: student loans come in two kinds, federal and private.
lines.say: Step one: student loans come in two kinds, federal and private.

lines.text: Federal loans come from the Education Department, with safety nets: income-based plans, forgiveness, and pauses when life goes sideways.
lines.say: Federal loans come from the Education Department, with safety nets: income-based plans, forgiveness, and pauses when life goes sideways.

lines.text: Private loans come from banks, credit unions and online lenders. You get the contract's terms, and none of the federal programs.
lines.say: Private loans come from banks, credit unions, and online lenders. You get the contract's terms, and none of the federal programs.

lines.text: Most student debt is federal: about $1.7 trillion, held by about 42 million people (2026).
lines.say: Most student debt is federal. The Education Department reported about one point seven trillion dollars in federal loans in twenty twenty-six, held by about forty-two million people.

lines.text: To see your federal loans, log in at studentaid.gov: every loan, balance, rate and servicer.
lines.say: Log in at studentaid dot gov to see every federal loan, its balance, rate, and servicer.

lines.text: For private loans, your free credit report shows those too.
lines.say: For private loans, your free credit report shows those too.

lines.text: For every loan, write down: balance, rate, federal or private, and servicer.
lines.say: Write down four things for every loan: the balance, the interest rate, federal or private, and the servicer.

lines.text: New federal undergrad loans for 2026-27 carry a fixed 6.52% rate.
lines.say: New federal undergraduate loans for the twenty twenty-six to twenty-seven school year carry a fixed rate of six point five two percent.

lines.text: Chapter 2: Pick a repayment plan.
lines.say: Chapter two: pick a repayment plan.

lines.text: With federal loans, your bill depends on your plan. Since July 2026, the menu is different.
lines.say: With federal loans, your monthly bill depends on your plan, and since July twenty twenty-six, the menu looks different.

lines.text: New loans made on or after July 1, 2026 get two choices: Tiered Standard, or RAP.
lines.say: If you take out a new loan on or after July first, twenty twenty-six, you get two choices: the Tiered Standard plan, or RAP.

lines.text: Tiered Standard is fixed. Under $25,000: 10 years. Up to $50,000: 15 years.
lines.say: Tiered Standard is a fixed payment, and the term depends on your balance. Under twenty-five thousand dollars, it's ten years. Up to fifty thousand, fifteen years.

lines.text: Up to $100,000: 20 years. Above that: 25. Longer term, smaller bill, more interest overall.
lines.say: Up to a hundred thousand, twenty years, and above that, twenty-five. Bigger balance, longer runway, smaller monthly bill, more interest overall.

lines.text: The other option is RAP, the Repayment Assistance Plan: a slice of your adjusted gross income.
lines.say: The other option is RAP, the Repayment Assistance Plan. Your payment is a slice of your adjusted gross income.

lines.text: It runs from 1% to 10%, up 1 point per $10,000 of income, up to 10% above $100,000.
lines.say: It runs from one to ten percent, rising one point per ten thousand dollars of income, up to ten percent above a hundred thousand.

lines.text: Example: an adjusted gross income of $45,000 is in the 4% bracket.
lines.say: Let's do an example. Say your adjusted gross income is forty-five thousand dollars. That lands in the four percent bracket.

lines.text: 4% of $45,000 = $1,800 a year. Divided by 12: $150 a month.
lines.say: Four percent of forty-five thousand is eighteen hundred dollars a year, or a hundred fifty dollars a month.

lines.text: RAP takes $50 a month off per dependent. With one child: $100 a month.
lines.say: RAP takes fifty dollars a month off for each dependent. With one child, that's a hundred dollars a month.

lines.text: Surprise: the lowest RAP payment is $10 a month. Some older plans allowed $0.
lines.say: Here's a surprise: the lowest RAP payment is ten dollars a month. Some older plans allowed zero.

lines.text: Pay on time, and interest your payment doesn't cover is waived. The balance doesn't snowball.
lines.say: The upside: if you pay on time and your payment doesn't cover the interest, the unpaid part is waived. Your balance doesn't snowball.

lines.text: If your payment cuts principal by less than $50, the government matches the gap, up to $50 a month.
lines.say: And if your payment cuts principal by less than fifty dollars, the government adds the difference, up to fifty.

lines.text: What's left after 360 qualifying payments, 30 years, is forgiven.
lines.say: Whatever's left after three hundred sixty qualifying payments, that's thirty years, is forgiven.

lines.text: Borrowed before July 2026? You also have income-based repayment (IBR) and the old standard plans.
lines.say: Borrowed before July twenty twenty-six? You also have income-based repayment, or I B R, and the older standard plans.

lines.text: PAYE and ICR are closing. Borrowers must move to IBR or RAP by July 1, 2028.
lines.say: Two older plans, PAYE and ICR, are closing. Borrowers in them must move to IBR or RAP by July first, twenty twenty-eight.

lines.text: SAVE is ending. In Dec 2025, the Education Department announced a settlement with Missouri to end it.
lines.say: And the SAVE plan is ending. In December twenty twenty-five, the Education Department announced a settlement with Missouri to shut it down.

lines.text: About 7 million SAVE borrowers sat in forbearance, with interest building since Aug 2025.
lines.say: About seven million borrowers sat in SAVE forbearance, with interest building since August twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: From July 2026, servicers sent notices with 90 days to pick a plan. Check yours for your date.
lines.say: Starting in July twenty twenty-six, servicers gave SAVE borrowers ninety days to pick a new plan, so check your notice for your exact date.

lines.text: No choice? You get placed in a standard plan, usually the highest monthly payment.
lines.say: If you don't choose, you get placed in a standard plan, which usually has the highest monthly payment.

lines.text: Parent PLUS loans aren't eligible for RAP. Check studentaid.gov for their options.
lines.say: Parent PLUS loans aren't eligible for RAP, so check studentaid dot gov for their options.

lines.text: Most new Parent PLUS borrowing is capped at $20,000 a year and $65,000 total per student, from July 2026.
lines.say: And most new Parent PLUS borrowing is capped at twenty thousand dollars a year and sixty-five thousand total, per student, starting July twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Chapter 3: Forgiveness and taxes.
lines.say: Chapter three: forgiveness and taxes.

lines.text: The big one: Public Service Loan Forgiveness, or PSLF.
lines.say: The big one is Public Service Loan Forgiveness, or P S L F.

lines.text: Make 120 qualifying monthly payments: 10 years, not necessarily in a row.
lines.say: The rules: make a hundred twenty qualifying monthly payments. That's ten years, and they don't have to be in a row.

lines.text: While working full time, 30+ hours a week, for a government employer or a 501(c)(3) nonprofit.
lines.say: While working full time, at least thirty hours a week, for a government employer or a five oh one c three nonprofit.

lines.text: Loans must be federal Direct Loans on a qualifying plan. RAP, IBR and the 10-year standard count.
lines.say: The loans must be federal Direct Loans, on a qualifying plan. RAP, I B R, and the ten-year standard plan all count.

lines.text: Through April 2026, about 1.25 million borrowers had about $93.4 billion forgiven.
lines.say: Through April twenty twenty-six, about one point two five million borrowers had about ninety-three billion dollars forgiven.

lines.text: A 2025 rule would have let the department disqualify some employers. Courts struck it down in June 2026.
lines.say: A twenty twenty-five rule would have let the department disqualify some employers, but courts struck it down in June twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: In Oct 2026, the department dropped 2 of its 3 appeals. Check your employer with the PSLF tool at studentaid.gov.
lines.say: In October twenty twenty-six, the department dropped two of its three appeals, so the old employer rules still applied that fall. Check yours with the P S L F tool at studentaid dot gov.

lines.text: PSLF forgiveness is federal tax-free. Income-driven plan forgiveness became taxable again in 2026.
lines.say: Now taxes. PSLF forgiveness is free of federal tax. But forgiveness at the end of an income-driven plan became taxable again in twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: On a 20- to 30-year path, forgiveness may come with a tax bill. Worth knowing early.
lines.say: So if you're on a twenty to thirty year path, forgiveness may come with a tax bill. Worth knowing early.

lines.text: Chapter 4: Pay it down faster, or refinance?
lines.say: Chapter four: pay it down faster, or refinance?

lines.text: Student loans have no prepayment penalty, federal or private.
lines.say: Not everyone wants to wait for forgiveness. Good news: student loans have no prepayment penalty, federal or private.

lines.text: When you pay extra, tell your servicer which loan gets it.
lines.say: One tip: when you pay extra, tell your servicer which loan gets it.

lines.text: Three loans: $4,000 federal at 5.5%, $9,000 federal at 6.53%, $7,000 private at 11%.
lines.say: Let's run real numbers. Three loans: four thousand dollars federal at five point five percent, nine thousand federal at six point five three, and seven thousand private at eleven percent.

lines.text: 10-year minimums: about $242. Add $200 extra: about $442 a month.
lines.say: Ten-year minimums add up to about two hundred forty-two dollars. Add two hundred extra, and it's about four hundred forty-two a month.

lines.text: Minimums only: about $9,060 in interest over 10 years. Our math.
lines.say: Paying only the minimums, you'd pay about nine thousand sixty dollars in interest over ten years. That's our math.

lines.text: Where does the extra $200 go? Avalanche: highest rate first. Snowball: smallest balance first.
lines.say: So where does the extra two hundred go? Avalanche means highest rate first. Snowball means smallest balance first.

lines.text: Avalanche: the 11% private loan goes first. Interest: about $3,327. Debt-free in 53 months.
lines.say: With the avalanche, the eleven percent private loan goes first. Total interest is about three thousand three hundred twenty-seven dollars, and you're debt-free in fifty-three months.

lines.text: Snowball: the $4,000 loan goes first. Interest: about $3,840. Done in 54 months.
lines.say: With the snowball, the four thousand dollar loan goes first. Total interest is about three thousand eight hundred forty, and you're done in fifty-four months.

lines.text: The avalanche saves about $512 and one month of payments. Our math.
lines.say: So the avalanche saves about five hundred twelve dollars and a month of payments, in our math.

lines.text: But the snowball clears its first loan in month 18, versus month 27.
lines.say: But the snowball clears its first loan in month eighteen, versus month twenty-seven. That quick win keeps some people going.

lines.text: The math favors the avalanche. The best plan is the one you'll stick with.
lines.say: Which is better? The math favors the avalanche, but the best plan is the one you'll stick with.

lines.text: Either way, interest drops from about $9,060 to under $4,000.
lines.say: Either way, interest drops from about nine thousand dollars to under four thousand.

lines.text: Consolidating and refinancing get mixed up, and the difference is huge.
lines.say: People mix up consolidating and refinancing, and the difference is huge.

lines.text: Consolidation is a free federal program at studentaid.gov that rolls federal loans into one.
lines.say: Consolidation is a federal program. It's free at studentaid dot gov, and it rolls your federal loans into one.

lines.text: It doesn't lower your rate: it's the weighted average, rounded up to the nearest 1/8 of a percent.
lines.say: But it doesn't lower your rate. The new rate is the weighted average of the old ones, rounded up to the nearest eighth of a percent.

lines.text: Our two federal loans average 6.213%. Rounded up, the new rate is 6.25%.
lines.say: Take our two federal loans. The weighted average is six point two one three percent. Rounded up, the new rate is six point two five.

lines.text: Consolidate on or after July 1, 2026, and your plans narrow to RAP or Tiered Standard.
lines.say: And here's a catch: consolidate on or after July first, twenty twenty-six, and your plan choices narrow to RAP or Tiered Standard.

lines.text: Refinancing: a private lender pays off your loans with a new private loan, maybe at a lower rate.
lines.say: Refinancing is different: a private lender pays off your loans with a new private loan, maybe at a lower rate.

lines.text: Refinancing federal loans is a one-way door. You can't turn them back into federal loans.
lines.say: If you refinance federal loans, it's a one-way door. You can't turn them back into federal loans.

lines.text: You'd lose RAP and IBR, PSLF, federal hardship pauses, and federal death and disability discharge.
lines.say: You'd give up RAP and I B R, P S L F, federal hardship pauses, and federal discharge for death or disability.

lines.text: Loans already private have no federal perks to lose, so rate and terms are the main trade-off.
lines.say: For loans already private, there are no federal perks to lose, so rate and terms are the main trade-off.

lines.text: Chapter 5: Default and scams.
lines.say: Chapter five: default and scams.

lines.text: A federal loan defaults after 270 days of missed payments.
lines.say: A federal loan goes into default after two hundred seventy days of missed payments.

lines.text: Default: the whole balance can come due, and it lands on your credit report.
lines.say: Default means the whole balance can come due at once, and the default lands on your credit report.

lines.text: The government can also take tax refunds and garnish up to 15% of disposable pay, after 30+ days' notice.
lines.say: The government can also take your tax refund and garnish up to fifteen percent of your disposable pay, after at least thirty days' notice.

lines.text: In Jan 2026, the Education Department paused wage garnishment and tax refund seizures. No restart date as of Nov 2026.
lines.say: In January twenty twenty-six, the Education Department paused wage garnishment and tax refund seizures. As of November twenty twenty-six, no restart date had been announced.

lines.text: Paused isn't forgiven. Defaults still hit credit reports, and collections can restart. Check studentaid.gov.
lines.say: But paused isn't forgiven. Defaults still hit credit reports, and collections can restart, so check the current status at studentaid dot gov.

lines.text: The main way out: rehabilitation. 9 on-time payments within 10 months, set by your income.
lines.say: The main way out is rehabilitation: nine on-time payments within ten months, with the amount based on your income.

lines.text: Finish it, and the default record comes off your credit report. Earlier late payments stay.
lines.say: Finish it, and the default record comes off your credit report, though the earlier late payments stay.

lines.text: Right now you get one rehabilitation. Starting July 2027, the law allows two.
lines.say: Right now you get one rehabilitation. Starting in July twenty twenty-seven, the law allows two.

lines.text: The other route: consolidating out of default. Faster, but the default stays in your credit history.
lines.say: The other route is consolidating out of default. It's faster, but the default stays in your credit history.

lines.text: Last trap: scams. What debt relief companies sell for federal loans is free at studentaid.gov or your servicer.
lines.say: Last trap: scams. Everything a debt relief company sells for federal loans is free at studentaid dot gov, or from your servicer.

lines.text: Red flags: upfront fees, which the FTC says are illegal before a company helps you, and instant forgiveness promises.
lines.say: Red flags: upfront fees, which the F T C says are illegal before a company helps you, and promises of instant forgiveness.

lines.text: Asking for your FSA ID, or claiming ties to the Education Department. Report them at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
lines.say: Others ask for your F S A I D login, or claim ties to the Education Department. Report them at report fraud dot F T C dot gov.

lines.text: Chapter 6: The checklist.
lines.say: Chapter six: the checklist.

lines.text: List every loan with its rate, and mark it federal or private.
lines.say: Here's the one-screen checklist. List every loan with its rate, and mark it federal or private.

lines.text: Check which plan you're in, especially after SAVE, and run the RAP math on your income.
lines.say: Check which plan you're in, especially if you were on SAVE, and run the RAP math on your own income.

lines.text: In public service? Confirm your employer and track your 120 payments. Then aim extra money at one loan at a time.
lines.say: In public service? Confirm your employer and track your hundred twenty payments. Then aim extra money at one loan at a time.

lines.text: Treat refinancing federal loans as permanent, and never pay for help that's free.
lines.say: Treat refinancing federal loans as permanent, and never pay anyone for help that's free.

lines.text: Key numbers: RAP takes 1% to 10% of income. PSLF takes 120 payments.
lines.say: Two key numbers: RAP takes one to ten percent of your income, and P S L F takes a hundred twenty payments.

lines.text: Falling behind? Act before day 270. Every option is easier before default.
lines.say: And if you're falling behind, act before day two hundred seventy. Every option is easier before default than after.

lines.say: Over one in ten student loan dollars is seriously late. Knowing the rules is how you stay out of that number.

post.yt_desc:
In the third quarter of 2026, 10.9% of US student loan balances were 90+ days delinquent or in default, and total student debt reached $1.656 trillion (New York Fed, Nov 2026). Federal repayment rules changed under the July 2025 budget law: the Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) launched July 1, 2026, the SAVE plan is ending, PAYE and ICR close by July 1, 2028, and new Parent PLUS limits apply. This guide covers federal vs private loans, the Tiered Standard plan and RAP with worked math, PSLF (120 payments, tax-free) and the June 2026 court rulings on employer rules, avalanche vs snowball on a $20,000 example (our math), consolidation vs refinancing, getting out of default, and how to spot scams.

CHAPTERS

Sources: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Household Debt and Credit reports (Q3 2019-Q3 2026; Nov 10, 2026); Federal Student Aid Data Center (2026); FSA 2026-27 interest rate announcement (June 2026); U.S. Department of Education RAP fact sheet and Jan 16, 2026 collections announcement; NPR (Dec 2025, June 2026); Congressional Research Service on PSLF (Aug 2026); NASFAA (2026); FTC consumer guidance on student loan scams.

News and education, not financial advice.
